newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Ex-hostage makes "weird" return to Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ex-hostage makes "weird" return to Lebanon.

text.p: It was weird going back to Baalbek where he had been kept shackled in a damp basement, and even more unsettling interviewing the man who may have given orders to his captors.
But for Terry Anderson, the journalist held hostage in Lebanon for nearly seven years, facing down his past was more a workaday necessity than therapy.
Forgiveness is not the theme of a documentary Anderson has made to mark the fifth anniversary of his release. He says it is essential for the world to understand why he was kidnapped.
"I wanted to go back to Lebanon, but I wanted to go back for a reason, not just as a tourist," he said in an interview in London after his first visit back to the country.

"Most people, Americans and others, have a really outdated and simplistic view of Lebanon. They think it's all war, kidnapping, bombs," said Anderson, who has filled out comfortably from the haggard man whose photographs, released by the kidnappers, told of the hardships of his captivity.
"That's not really what Lebanon is all about."
LONGEST-HELD AND LAST TO BE FREED

Anderson was the longest-held of the Beirut hostages. Bundled into a car on his way to play tennis one March morning in 1985, he was not freed until December 5, 1991 -- the last of the foreigners let go by Islamic fundamentalist kidnappers.
Anderson is not so much interested in his kidnappers' motives as he is in helping the world get to grips with the social and political background that gave rise to them.
"You are never going to be able to deal with it unless you understand it," he said.

To address this issue he had to go to Baalbek, one of the centres of Shi'ite fundamentalism in Lebanon and a headquarters of Hizbollah, the "Party of God" that has become an important political force in Lebanon.
Hizbollah is also widely suspected of backing Islamic Jihad, the shadowy group that kidnapped foreigners in the 1980s.
Anderson met Hizbollah's spiritual leader Sheikh Hassan Nasrallah at his Baalbek office, within sight of the Sheikh Abdullah barracks where he was sometimes kept chained.

The 45-minute documentary shows their meeting -- polite but cool. Anderson, a former bureau chief with the Associated Press news agency, questions Nasrallah repeatedly about whether he approved of the kidnappings, and gets only noncommittal answers from the black-robed cleric.
"It was weird," Anderson said of the interview.
"It was strange, mostly because they haven't changed. They are still soft, smiling, yet underneath hard-as-rock people."
"It was part of the job. If it hadn't been for the film I wouldn't have done it."

Anderson was a little surprised to see how Baalbek had changed. Tourists were clambering on the once-deserted ruins of Heliopolis, some of the finest Roman ruins in the world. Women walked the streets without headscarves -- a rare sight in 1985, when Hizbollah gripped that part of eastern Lebanon.
"They have changed tactics greatly. They are no longer trying to impose their beliefs on other people. They can't," Anderson said. "But they still have the same world view."
There were some questions Anderson did not ask.
"I don't know if any of those people were directly involved on my kidnapping or those of others," he said.
"Nasrallah was a senior person in Hizbollah. I suspect he was around in the hierarchy. And I am not really interested," he added. "They are no longer part of my life."

Anderson graphically documented his ordeal in a book, "Den of Lions". Wrapped in reels and reels of tape, he was transported from prison to prison in a secret compartment underneath a truck, terrified he would expire from the fumes.

He and fellow hostages such as Thomas Sutherland, Brian Keenan, Terry Waite and John McCarthy were regularly beaten but say the worst agony was the boredom imposed by a lack of reading material and frequent solitary confinement.
Asked why he had no hard feelings, Anderson answered: "It's always been hard for people to understand that."
He mentions Phan Thi Kim Phuc, who, as a nine-year-old, was photographed running screaming down a road in her Vietnamese village during a 1972 U.S. napalm attack.
Now 32, she visited the Vietnam War memorial in Washington last month (Nov 11). Horribly scarred from her burns, Phan nonetheless spoke in a conciliatory tone.

"Even if I could talk face-to-face with the pilot who dropped the bombs, I could tell him we cannot change history but we should try to do good things for the present and for the future to promote peace," she said.
LEBANESE TIES

Anderson said he had even more reason to lose any hard feelings. He is married to a Lebanese woman, Madeleine, and their daughter Sulome is half-Lebanese. He chose to live in Beirut long after most Westerners had left.
"I like the Lebanese. I like the country," he says. "In many ways, the Lebanese are admirable. They had a war. They did many bad things to each other. That happens in a war."
The Lebanese people could not be blamed for the kidnappings, he added. "Individuals commit crimes. Nations and peoples don't."
Anderson, who now teaches at New York's Columbia University, lectures, and campaigns for the Committee to Protect Journalists, says he has better things to do than hold grudges.
"I have a good life. I am happy. Why should I keep all that anger? I don't need that in my life."
Anderson visited Madeleine's family, saw old friends in Beirut and south Lebanon and interviewed the country's billionaire prime minister, Rafik Hariri. Overall, his impressions are hopeful.
"They're making progress. I don't think civil war has a chance of breaking out again. They don't want to hate each other any more," he said.

But, says the ex-Marine and Vietnam war veteran, who covered Israel's invasion of Lebanon and the 1983 bombing of the U.S. Marines barracks that killed 241: "It's nice to do an optimistic story once in a while."
